First, I provided some examples of command hallucinations from a fictional detective named Bowman in a book called "The Silent Room" by Mari Hannah. Command hallucinations are when a person hears a voice or voices telling them to do something, which can be anything from a simple command to a threat.

Next, I discussed olfactory phantosmia and parosmia, which are distortions to the sense of smell. Olfactory phantosmia is when a person smells an odor that is not actually there, while parosmia is when a person inhales a real odor but perceives it as a different scent than remembered. These conditions can result from a range of conditions, including nasal infections, nasal polyps, dental problems, migraines, head injuries, seizures, strokes, or brain tumors. Environmental exposures, such as smoking or exposure to certain chemicals, can also cause these distortions.

Finally, I shared some statistics about the decline in leisure reading among young people in the United States. According to a study by Jean M. Twenge, the number of high school seniors who read for pleasure has dropped from 60% in the 1970s to 19% in the mid-2010s. Twelfth-graders also read an average of two fewer books per year in the mid-2010s than in the mid-1970s, and a third did not read any books at all (including e-books) compared to one-ninth in the 1970s. These gaps were consistent across sexual, racial, and socioeconomic lines. The study also found that the decline in leisure reading was unexpected because of the convenience of electronic devices like tablets, which allow for easy access to books and magazines.
